newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australians welcomes PM's attack on race.
newsitem.headline: Australians welcomes PM's attack on race.

text.p: Australian political and business leaders on Friday welcomed a strong public attack by Prime Minister John Howard's on race row politician Pauline Hanson, but said he should have acted earlier.

The country's richest businesswoman, Janet Holmes a Court, and Labor opposition leaders said the divisive national race row sparked by Hanson had undermined Australia's international standing and put jobs at risk.
Former foreign minister Gareth Evans, now an opposition leader, said Howard had only been stung into action by polls showing Hanson's fledgling party had grabbed 10 percent opinion voter support.
"What he said was long, long overdue," Evans said in a radio interview.

"He didn't say anything when it was the decent thing to say. He didn't say anything when Australia's international reputation was first put at risk. He didn't say anything when Australia's trade and jobs were being put at risk.
"He's only said something now when the opinion polls have come out and coalition votes have been put at risk."
Howard on Thursday launched his strongest attack so far on Hanson, an independent MP who sparked a national row with a campaign against Asian immigration and Aboriginal welfare.
Howard, who had largely tried to ignore her until now, accused Hanson of exploiting fear and instability and threatening links with the booming economies of Asia.
"The Hanson cure would be worse than the disease," Howard told a Sydney dinner to launch a branch of the U.S-Asia Society.
"The political campaign mounted by the member for Oxley (Hanson) seeks to exploit fear and instability without offering solutions for hope."
Holmes a Court, who is also a central bank director, said Australians should seize the opportunity offered by Howard's attack to put the race row genie back in the bottle.
"There are a lot of people trying to push it back in the bottle -- and I think there was an opportunity to have stopped it earlier in its tracks, but that wasn't taken," she said.
"I'm hopeful that as more and more of our government politicians and more and more people in the community are expressing their outrage that it'll go right back in (the bottle) again."
